notes.meaning: About four months after hearing about Jerusalem's broken walls, Nehemiah was serving wine to King Artaxerxes. Persian court rules required servants to look cheerful before the king, and Nehemiah had never shown sadness in the royal presence before. His long wait shows that he spent months in patient prayer before God opened a door to speak.

The king noticed Nehemiah's gloomy face and kindly asked what was troubling his heart, since he was not physically sick. Nehemiah was suddenly terrified. Showing grief could look like discontent with the king, and Artaxerxes had previously stopped work on Jerusalem's walls.

Nehemiah politely wished the king long life and explained why he was grieving. He stated that the city where his ancestors were buried lay in ruins with burned gates. In the Persian world, honoring family tombs was deeply respected, so Nehemiah wisely focused on that rather than politics.

The king asked Nehemiah what favor he wanted to request. Before speaking a single word, Nehemiah offered a quick, silent prayer to God. His months of private prayer gave him the reflex to rely on God in that split-second decision.

Nehemiah humbly asked the king for permission to go to Judah and rebuild his ancestral city. He framed his request with great respect, asking only if it pleased the king. He did not ask someone else to go, but stepped forward to take on the difficult task himself.

With the queen sitting beside him in what seems to have been a private setting, the king asked how long the trip would take and when he would return. Nehemiah gave him a specific timeline, and the king granted his leave. Good faith in God goes hand in hand with clear, thoughtful planning.

Nehemiah asked for official royal letters addressed to the governors west of the Euphrates River. These letters would grant him safe passage and travel supplies as he moved through foreign territories toward Judah. He used the legal authority available to him to protect his mission.

Nehemiah also asked for an order to Asaph, the keeper of the royal forest, to provide timber for the temple fortress gates, the city walls, and his own residence. The king granted all these requests because God was guiding the king's heart. Nehemiah gave God full credit for this great breakthrough.

Nehemiah traveled west of the Euphrates and delivered the royal letters to the local governors. The king had also sent cavalry and army officers to accompany him. This military escort gave him protection on the long journey and showed the regional rulers that he carried royal authority.

Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official were very angry when they heard about Nehemiah. They ruled nearby areas and did not want the Jewish people to become strong and secure again. Whenever God begins to move his people toward renewal, enemies often rise up to oppose it.

Nehemiah arrived in Jerusalem and stayed there quietly for three days. After traveling roughly eight hundred miles, he took time to rest, pray, and assess the situation before doing any public work. Taking time to pause and seek God is essential before starting any big endeavor.

Nehemiah went out secretly at night with only a few trusted companions and a single riding animal. He kept his mission quiet so enemies would not sabotage the plan before it even began. He recognized that the burden to rebuild was something God had placed directly into his heart.

Under cover of darkness, Nehemiah rode out through the Valley Gate toward the Serpent Well and the Dung Gate. He carefully examined the smashed walls and the gates that had been burned to ashes. He wanted to see the full extent of the damage with his own eyes.

He continued his survey toward the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool. There was so much fallen stone and broken rubble that his animal could not pass through the ruins. The wreckage showed just how severe Jerusalem's destruction had been.

Nehemiah moved on foot along the Kidron Valley in the dark to examine the rest of the wall. After finishing his inspection around the city, he returned and re-entered through the Valley Gate. He now had the exact facts he needed to lead the people effectively.

The local Jewish leaders, priests, nobles, and workers still had no idea where Nehemiah had gone or what he was planning. He kept everything private until his plan was ready. Wise leaders protect their plans from idle gossip and early discouragement.

Nehemiah gathered the Jewish leaders and pointed out their shared hardship, showing them that the ruined city brought shame to God's people. He did not point fingers or blame them for past failures, but said, 'Come, let us rebuild.' He invited everyone to unite and remove their public disgrace.

Nehemiah encouraged the leaders by sharing how God had guided him and what King Artaxerxes had promised. Hearing of God's favor and the king's royal backing stirred the people's faith. They eagerly replied, 'Let us start rebuilding,' and threw themselves into the work.

Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem the Arab heard about the project and began to mock the workers. They sneered at the Jews and falsely accused them of rebelling against the Persian emperor. Opponents often use fear and false charges to halt godly work.

Nehemiah answered his critics with firm faith, declaring that the God of heaven would give his servants success. He also told the mockers plainly that they had no historical, legal, or religious share in Jerusalem. God's people find their courage in his promise, not in the approval of their opponents.
